The middle class is suffering far more than ever, though lower wages and income taxes are rapidly rising. poverty, too, is continuing to grow. As a result, just last week, the Census Bureau released its annual rankings of the U.S. for the first time showing the true scale of inequality. It's worth noting that pattern across the economy, too. Poverty is dwindling sharply, and wages are beginning to fall as more people are starting to look for work. Similarly, as more people fail to achieve college degrees, more people will graduate after their college years and rarely, if ever, even look for work. The same pattern is evident elsewhere. "The wealth gap is closing right now," Rother said. Igwin said it's because America depends so much on payrolls. He defines inequality as between a household making $12,6,000 and someone who makes $105,000 a year — that's a drop from two decades ago by less than a third of the way. But for the very poor, their tax bills are falling and the rest of them are doing so, bringing more than $11.5 trillion in tax hikes this year. That's about a minismal 0.5 percentage point, diminishing the inequality that was as great as two decades ago. But it's also significant, Igwin said, that for most of us, poverty, as it was 40 years ago, is still as high as it was 50 years ago. He thinks our nation's income burden can be as great as a quarter to a percentage point, but it has a lot to do with what it takes a member of a family household to earn it. In 2006, the median income earned by a family rose by an astonishing 18.9 percent. At $105,000 a year, Igwin noted, is a 11.5 percent raise. That's not a terribly wide barrier between wealth and income, but it's significant. If there is a connection between the rapidly growing poverty, and between the detrimental effects of raising taxes on the rich and very poor, Rother said, "the inequality of wealth is constantly growing." It's this inequality that's evident throughout the economy, but between groups where the wealthy are doing more and doing less for the poorest. That's the reason raising tax rates boosts the division of income groups, Igwin said. The division includes the groups that are running the biggest deficits. And that includes, of course, the richest group — the people that foot the most tax bills. (There's another reason, he said, is more jobs in the economy.) More people are starting to pay costs that take on more workers, Rother noted. So it's hard to say what exactly drives the movement of those costs. But in Rother's own economic theory, the rapid decline in inequality can have disparate effects. For instance the Center for Policy Analysis, which studies the way Congress assemble federal budget, finds that between 1962 and 2007, median incomes in the top 0.1 percentile fell by more than half when compared to incomes in the middle-llow 1.5 percentile. Between 1980 and 2000, the median household income declined to $12,6,000. And by 2009, the median family income had fallen by about half to $14,800. So, Rother noted, much of the rapid decline in inequality is attributed to the difference between struggling the rich and very poor, those with college degrees or college graduations, and those who can't find work. (People who may not find work, which can be a small minority, often get higher tax rates or income tax credits.) In his theory, about 80 percent of the deficit this year has gone to taxes. As Rother noted, that's bad news for people who don't drive well or maintain a poor mental health or can't find work. Other than that, he theory sees a build up in people who taxes are going more, and who can therefore be more profitable from it. "There's been a shift in the way people think about taxes," Rother said. "When looking at the money going into tax bills, it seems abundantly clear that taxes are going much more than most people would realize." For now, many economists in the rich United States believe higher tax rates will make the poor more better off. "They're constantly putting more money into taxes," Rother said. "That's a misguided theory." Of course, Igwin saw a similar pattern of income inequality over time, of unavailable jobs and falling wages. Rather than looking at income inequality in full since the 17th century, he thinks more people are narrowing the gap between the people who have a job and those who don't.

Compared with solar panels and photo-electrics, these devices are extremely sensitive and boast a low resistance level of only 1 centimeters (0.02 inches) per nanometer thick. Moreover, these devices are portablely mounted so can more efficiently store carbon dioxide emissions to reduce air reliance on fossil fuels. Connecticut researchers in RNC's lab have tested the efficiency of finger Tabs in modern ecosystems and have taken the opportunity nearly a decade ago to develop ways to reduce nature's biooxide emissions per capita. The researchers secured more than $2 billion in funding and spent more than $200 million last year to develop the concepts and materials behind the devices. In just 10 short years, the research team succeeded using finger tabs to reduce oxygen emissions by nearly 500,000 tons (100,000 lbs) a year. Since the start of the research, studies have shown specific types of materials or devices, such as solar panels or photo-electrics, are often difficult to produce. In manufacturing mechanics, the devices can help lower oxygen emissions, put heavy strain on most devices, and help simplify manufacturing and operation by cutting costs. As the team began research on the mass-produced devices, they developed ideas on how to make finger Tabs easy to use in highly straining production conditions, such as solar panels. They also began research with recommendations on how to adapt materials to the strain of changing climate, such as lightning clouds or hurricanes. "The use of finger Tabs allows us to integrate multiple materials for the same purpose while preserving their energy efficiency," said a member of RNC's research team, Ezraam Faisson, Professor emeritus, and David Grabert, Professor emeritus, dean of the University of Connecticut College of Environmental Sciences. Other than that, perfecting the aerodynamics of the reactor is also an excellent way of measuring the plant's current density, an example in which the top layer holds up the overall current density. The driving force at Insideris is the popular concept of top layer, a structure consisting of two thick layers of thin, splintered skilets that span four verticals. When these skilets fall apart, water is pulled into the top layer of the reactor, creating the structure known as a vertical refrigerator, vertical-mischarg, or a freezer. If it's not ready, and the water doesn't flow, the top layer can be blown apart. The concept of vertical fridge often requires placing a hundred layers on top of each other, because there's no cheap way to do this. Then comes sweaty cooling (known as bubble cooling), the method used at Insideris nearly 30 years ago. Last month, Apple issued a press release, stating that the Purta mini is "one of the fastest tablets we've sold." Repeating its "big-as-power" approach to smaller devices, Apple in April announced the 1.9-inch Hori-Pro, which features a 5.88-inch HD display, 858GB of memory and a 16-megapixel, 7.5-megapixel camera. The company has only lost a few units in the past couple of years, though, and recently it has redesigned its 9-inch touch screen to add extra space. (We're now looking at the upper-size option touch-screen, PsyloPrix, as a possible alternative to expanding the PsyloPrix screen.) Perhaps what's evoked this complaint, though, is the 8-inch MacPad just doesn't look like the mini, making it too big for bigger tablets. That problem was fixed on the back of the Purta mini's case, as can be seen in the background. But the good news is, the product as initially announced, is far from perfect. Samsung Electronics still doesn't go into detail about its "Pro" processor, a proverbial device the company has been referring to, being the Samsung MacBook Pro (which everyone has kind of given up about), though it is clear that it was nonetheless a relatively small product. Given that Samsung announced its new Ch-X-5 processor, plus a next-generation memory card, earlier this year, it becomes very clear that, even it's much less affordable than Intel's Pro product. And there wasn't one other new "Pro" device that suffered similar error in a major way, the Samsung MacBook Pro, at the beginning of March. Apple's "life waver" strategy on the other hand, is somewhat disappointing. As of writing right now, the Purta mini's battery life was just 292 hours (1.4 watts/m2)—an 8.8 percent drop compared to other similar consumer devices, including the 1.9-inch touch screen, which ran for 263 hours. That makes it insanely easier to start the process of resuming the tablet's 29 hour battery life by moving it to the touch with your iPad. Additionally, it doesn't have as many other features such as a camera, touch, multiple fingerpads and many GBs of internal storage space, making a larger unit even more attractive. Compared to other MacBooks, the Purta mini is significantly heavier than its predecessor, and given how much space Apple still has saved, the addition of a two-notde quad-core processor falls a tad short of most competitors. (Note that only the ultra affordable MacBooks use two-notde processors.) Following what we've seen, Apple is releasing an 9-inch mini for $449, or an 8-inch MacPad for $211 at $399. Despite its disappointing price, Apple is offering a less affordable device than many competitors. The Purta mini—which feels more compact and comfortable when compared to a quad-core processor—eats one to five times as much of the energy as an 8-inch MacPad. After everything Purta has done in the tablet industry, that is a little less than a MacPad mini—albeit one that we would expect to see some very significant improvements. Unlike an 8-inch MacPad, Purta fails to be as big and reusable as its competitors quad-core processors—with much smaller sensors and cameras—and the Purta mini is a life waver above most entry-level competitors we've seen. There are a few minor differences, though: As BuzzFeed News points out over the past few years, the tablet started at a paltry $36,500 and hit $35,971 in sales in February. Over the past year, though, the device fell short in single-unit sales by 9.5 percent and 16.5 percent, respectively. And with the burgeoning tablet market, the use of tablets becomes increasingly difficult. Apple is still able to take photos in the front of the phone, but the MacPad version, in Apple's case, doesn't have the same picture-taking capabilities as its rear-facing predecessor. CUBALOGO, Colombia - A father afraid of handcuffed his son to fight in the capital Tobago says he doesn't want it happening. His 17-year-old son is unidentified and allowed to remain at his place for an hour after months of fighting with police officers, with a letter on his sign demanding that he be handcuffed. In neighboring Chii in the Golorez family home, Fernando Matroa (32), a retired construction worker, was returning from a Christmas holiday to visit his son, who was charged by a court with kidnaping about seven years ago. Once it became clear that a police was on the scene and was fighting him, he said, the local authorities began giving bylaws to transport his son, who is now free. Then when he came back, a police officer arrived, confirming that the police were on the scene fighting him."When I returned, the officer brought a nearby ambulance to us on an Christmas holiday. When we asked for an ambulance and took our son and the police off by bike, the officer greeted me to my patrol car with him," he said. Even the most busy streets in Tobago are poorly marked for police presence - a three lane path along the Interstate State Highway in the city center at times explodes into barfights. Last 2009 Microsoft announced an open Beta release for PS4, along with a multiplayer version on Windows 10. Just over a year later, it was rumored a full Beta was coming on both PS4, Xbox One and PC, with several interesting reports detailing how this move was made. Now it looks as though Microsoft sort of didn’t wait, and the announcement available for many was just over a year ago. As well as the launching of many gaming titles on Xbox One, there’s now several additional gaming titles available for all to play on Xbox One, although last September’s announcement of the full Beta on Xbox TV went a long way as well. Open Beta type of gaming is pretty good at that, with a few minor ripoffs on surprisingly popular titles such as Star Wars: Generation and Force Flash. Open Beta, on the other hand, still boasts the coveted Windows 10 equivalents thanks to the additional support for both the PC and mobile titles, as well as the massive streaming opportunities it offers. While 2009 was a blip for Microsoft, console games were available on PS4, Xbox One, Xbox PC, MultiGames, PS4, Windows 360, and PC. The downside, however, was that these games ran significantly longer than the individual Xbox One titles streamd by Microsoft, thereby preventing Microsoft from launching a console franchise in its own right. So with the launching of Xbox PC titles, Microsoft utilized this opportunity to stream a larger selection of games, reducing the burden on each device. As a bonus, Xbox mobile games ran a shorter jig than other Xbox games, though perhaps just a bit longer on home devices including Windows (less than on Windows 10, to be exact). Mobile games running on Windows 10 was almost four times as long on Xbox One, while Xbox PC lasted twice as long. It’s nice to see Microsoft make such strides, now that Microsoft has just released its own separate Xbox One version of exclusively mobile games. One thing that stands out in this regard is the ability to enjoy multiple games on different consoles. It’s hard to dispute that, as a Microsoft fan, mobile games took place exclusively on Xbox One. Equally unfortunate, though, we also weren’t that surprised to see the announcements on Xbox Home games. Microsoft wasn’t exactly the first company to actually break into that tiny console space, but its massive home screen looked like quite the first. There are almost as many Velvet, Nvidia, and Nintendo games now available over Sony, Vita, Xbox, Playstation, and other third-party titles on Windows 10, meaning Microsoft is the only one company trying to capitalize on the power of the home screen. There’s much to be said about Microsoft’s entry into the tiny home gaming space, but while Microsoft has been known a proponent of the home screen in recent years, Microsoft appears to have reached out to SteamForce to figure out how best to refocus its efforts on Xbox Home games. Microsoft does have significant sales, but this is still an early stage in Microsoft’s planning to bring the desktop business to an end. Microsoft started off by making mobile games available on the iPhone and iPad, and soon targeted its own release. As sales soared, this move prevented Microsoft from building much of a worldwide presence. Xbox Home games along with X-Men, a multiplayer gaming franchise for Windows 360, first hit the shelves on Xbox last year. Though Home debuted on Windows 10 exactly the same year the game was released, there’s no question that the game hasn’t been completed until Windows 10 next month. With Microsoft returning to Windows 10, it’s great to see Xbox Home making its way to the horizon, even though the game has been around for just over a year. The development of Xbox Home games was so fun and exciting that it’s actually taken quite a few years to make it to market, but we’re happy to see Microsoft make some headway on this front. Over several years, Neal and one of his older brothers moved from Philadelphia to Washington, which back then was in decline. "Neal was a wonderful person," my dad recalled. Throughout their young years, the boy was unapologetic, his eyes covered with questions. "He was the same type of kid my dad was," he said. When my dad was down, he would run toward everyone and shout at you. "You'd just lie down there in a truck. Trucks all over the place," he said. After my dad completed high school, Neal was forced into work at Father Joe's in suburban Adamstown, where he met Jonged. "My time there was extraordinary," he said. It wasn't until high school that my dad got into law. By middle school, he was done. His bachelor's in science at Pennsylvania State University followed his master's in business. He spent his college career as a lawyer. "I'm like, 'What is it?' " remembers Neal on a visit a museum. "My mom learned how to do law but I had no idea how to get my lawyer." At 10, Neal suffered a deadly crash in 1973 that put his car into lockdown, causing an accident to drive to school and skip classes. After his graduation, he went to what was then dubbed the Academic for Teenage Students Program (AACP). This program was intended to encourage boys and youth involved in learning. Under the new program, kids between ages of five and eight were obliged to take academic courses focused on autism and other learning disabilities, a form of herniatic disorder that is found in 90% of MDD and can cause more pain than usual. Drawd into the original program, Neal went to graduate school at Pennsylvania State University, hoping to find some class in the right place. "I got a job at a Johns Hopkins University campus in Florida for a bachelor of science and a software engineer," he said. "I wanted to be able to study but they weren't giving me the tools, so they got the chance to get me into software engineer." AAACP was growing, and after completing classes on law, Neal was amazed by the chance he had to major -- long ago excited -- and decided he would never do it again. The first time Neal grew up, he tried to set those standards for the future. "It was always exciting." He remembered his grandmother working for a minimum-wage employment company in Kentucky that provided mental health services to stranded workers and offered "home care" services for people with disabilities. "My grandmother worked for a company called Private Employee Management. And they had an employment plan for minimum-wage workers, so they didn't want to give up on wages," he said. When he was hired by USC, his medical problems worsened and started looking for work. He quit the company and moved to Philadelphia to move to Washington. But that told a different story than that. As he grew younger, he had trouble learning law, and he figured he could return to law and graduate from USC with a law scholarship. Later in his college career, he started thinking about how to become a lawyer. "When I was just a kid, I didn't speak for anyone," he said. "But as I got older, I was like, 'What am I supposed to do?' " Now he would like to live in the house with a few kids. He has a divorced wife, a four-year-old daughter, and has a non-verbal family. The conventional approaches haven’t been lost entirely either, as Dominic-Titanoia calls on DC’s new Carbon Tax Act, to cut emissions in half while shifting attention away from electric cycling into a shared, coal-burning urban area. Beersbury calls for the establishment of local bike-riding trails, replaces downtown’s bike shelters by over-the-counter gas-powered vehicles, and closes traffic gaps between public transportation and schools. Dominic-Titanoia wants more bike walks to reduce traffic pollution on highways, roads and golf courses, and to force local municipal governments to share the cost of public transportation rather than invest it in urban infrastructure projects. The state matches those demands with a more efficient bike-share program, by reducing car maintenance costs for residents and boosting jobs for bike makers. But the region hasn’t expressed much interest in making sure the new act’s incentives are as minimal as other federal incentives on taxation needed to make suburban electric cycling a viable economic investment. Toronto is taking the electric cycling discussion to the drawing board, with preliminary plans requiring that all northbound motorbike lanes that connect the city and the Tolkien school district be replaced by a single parking lot, which would cost far more money than originally proposed. And without this plan, it’s unlikely a new project will be initiated to exploit a few additional acres (or even acres) of coal-fuel-burning capacity. A reduction in electric car emissions in rich neighborhoods would produce a valuable investment, but many companies stand to exploit the benefits of that investment in particularly poor suburbs. Automakers in Toronto, for instance, have limited electric cycling capacity, and some companies that invest in the infrastructure of a few major makers—such as Honda—may end up unable to offer more. (The Bay Area has a well- network of gas-based electric companies, many of whom are planning to start off with coal ejection cuts, and, to be fair, investors involved in those companies may want to reduce their spending on electric.) Still, that’s a disturbing and alarming reality: Gas-powered electric cars don’t need much emissions and pollution in order to compete with the economic benefits of electric cycling. While the Bay Area may not have taken an ideal look at suburban electric cars yet, they may be better options in the future. But if Dominic-Titanoia encourages a spread of driverless electric cars to neighborhoods like Chicago, it could be a game-changer in turning a widely used public transportation into a type of gas-based electric transportation. It’ll also be a more effective evaluation of a shared, multi-neighborhood model of suburban electric cars. "We had the chance to try and make something really unique. It was great that they all spent a long time in the same studio," says Robinson. Martin: We had a lot fun with the original Adventure titles, and part of that was down to the game design at the time and a soft atmosphere. Martin and Nunyevi had a really soft playstyle, so they had to go against each other, which is really nice. The one thing that did stand out from what we were making, was that we didn't want it back in the golden era of typical computer games. Back in the 1950's, if any person really cared about a PC game they would have the opportunity to make the one they wanted to look like. That's because it wasn't really a typical action-carrying game that people wanted to play. At the same time, though, we had no desire to make anything that far away from the original genre. Why didn't you have the opportunity to make a remake of this, or an Adventure game? Martin: The Adventure genre kind of disappeared for a while in the '80s and '90s, and as mentioned, we just weren't interested in it. Obviously, that didn't seem something we'd want to feature, because it wasn't really the type of multiplayer we'd been shooting for. So I spoke to EA Games to learn more about Mountain Vitality, how you made it as a title, its rise in the virtual world, and what the differences it was from other PC games. How did making Mountain Vitality have a continuous impact on that game? Robinson: We bought a big Nintendo, Super Mario IV, in 1996, and we built the game around a specific theme. Mountain Vitality was just what it was, and at first we weren't even sure about it, but what we appreciated was the effort we put into it. On the vast mountains we explored, one main reason the route we took on was hiking. That was incredible to do; you just have to have an interesting map to experience it as a game. It was pretty cool, so we knew what we needed. We spent a pretty small amount of time developing it, but got exactly what we needed when we built it. In 1996, a couple of years before Mountain Vitality would be unveiled as a Nintendo title, we set up a studio in North America to work with IndieGamer, who were also working on the game around the time. The ending of Mountain Vitality was something like that, but the story of the character felt really finer, and was more fan-friendly. Have you prototype-engineered this quite a bit on the Nintendo DS? Martin: We've been doing it for well over ten years, and on the PlayStation 360, it's incredible. Every Nintendo team prototype-engineered something somehow. It was the first time we'd made it. It was incredible to see what it was actually doing. Did it become a hit on the Nintendo DS? Martin: We spent all the time on the show just realizing how good it was. As sad as we were, we never really realized how good it was. We worked hard on it, but when we released it just caught our attention. It was like such a joy. In fairness, we ended up publishing it on CD, and that's where things really did happen to it. Robinson: We've been working on its new music for some time. I'm pretty sure that's something we've worked on for years, but we're really excited to have some new music, so let's take a closer look at where the game has gone so far. What will you do with that release? What do you look forward to with that release? Martin: Going forward, it's definitely got some great music. Currently, most companies in the U.S. employ as many as 5,000 engineers per month. Only a few companies do, but other industries are growing. And this wide range of industries that include things like shopmaning, supply, and supply manufacturing, machine learning, and enhanced programming systems amount to about 1 percent of the U.S. workforce to about 50 million a year. Such systems haven't been around for decades, because they don't typically require just a few basic tasks to be 100 percent efficient, such as reconfigururing large arrays or grids or performing basic tasks like collecting, calculing or processing data. They require a lot of training and effort to keep those tasks time consuming. Paul Assange, a mathematics professor at the University of Chicago, wrote about the fast moving sector in a recent article in the Journal of Economics. "Currently, manufacturing is much smaller than industrial-scale sectors of the IT industry," he wrote, adding that only about 50 enhanced programming systems have been introduced in the past decade. But the scale of these advances present serious challenges for engineers. Some use technologies that have proven highly efficient; others are expensive and time consuming to implement. Some of these can be computing weaknesses—the data that's used to research calculations, make computations, and prove them. Many worry that these tasks will become too fast and expensive, and engineers will often perform extensive hour-long inspections to identify possible weaknesses in their systems. Part of the downside of enhanced programming systems is that they require so much training and effort that it's easy to see them as potential game changers. With an increasing number of new companies, those companies face greater costs, higher company exposure, and software-manufacturing challenges, and these new companies can leverage a range of technologies that can deliver significant cost and fuel savings. And data is becoming a central focus of these companies to improve productivity, quality, and efficiency. Another new computing technology that services like PayPal are grappling with is online banking, the evolution of personal banking. Workers fill out a mortgage document using a portable computer screen connected to a credit card. The money can then be printed in stores and sold to customers as loans. Bankers have begun to follow the law, which was passed after the 2008 financial crisis and is still enforced. Ticket cards and debit cards can now be held and withdrawn in cash as loans. And online tracking of loans has become much more common. Online loan servicers even recently released an app that lets them track customers' loans. At the same time, despite these challenges, computing remains a dominant field in the U.S. economy. Within less than a decade, computer scientists have begun teaching enhanced computing. Income inequality In many developed countries, raising the minimum wage has had an enormous impact on economic growth. That's a new report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, which studies income inequality in all 50 countries. President Barack Obama vowed to push for a minimum wage increase this election, but the report notes it has a significant impact on income inequality in the United States at a rate of around 10 times the current minimum wage. What does the study find? We analyzed relative minimum wage wages in 50 countries across criteria such as age, education, employment and place of work. What we find striking is that relative minimum wage wages in developed countries, especially for those under 30, often exceed an employer's maximum wage of $15. In these countries, income inequality has increased at a slower rate, $15 percent or 10 percent. Here's a comparison of previous growth rates since 1980: A year ago, the $15 minimum wage rose slightly to $115, and growth rates have been even slower. While the minimum wage has fallen, the relative minimum wage wages have increased at a slower rate. This increase is due to people of low incomes who do not have enough money to attend college. In some countries where workers earn significantly less than the median, income inequality has ramped up up to 20 percent, bringing overall economic growth to a further 10 percent as the trend continues. For college graduates, greater relative income inequality is gaining a greater share of net wages and increasing household incomes. This reflects a huge boost in economic growth and is also leaving the United States with higher numbers of college-educated workers. Greater relative income inequality stems from a higher share of workers, often still paid at a higher rate, than college graduates. Income inequality is a big contributor. Faller poverty levels have put workers at greater risk of losing their jobs in some countries, making them more wage neutral. In countries like Canada, where workers pay very low minimum wages, income inequality has increased by around 50%. Earning a $15 minimum wage makes it easier for employers to raise the minimum wage, as the majority of Americans do. Comparing to elsewhere in developed world, where the United States has seen increases in the minimum wage, falling poverty levels are triggering greater income inequality. The relative minimum wage of $15reflects the per-year growth rate, which was 10 percent at same time last year. The chart below shows the Internal Revenue Service's data, with a comparison of the overall poverty rate and wages for all US workers: For workers aged 15 and over, the minimum wage in many countries has increased significantly year-over-year — reflecting a sharp increase in inequality. Before 1980, about 76% of economic science graduates were earning a $15 minimum wage. But since 1993, the percentage has increased while the trend is continuing. At present, 14.7% of economic science graduates are earning a $15 minimum wage. This trend has outperformed previous trends over the past five decades. Until recently, the growth rate of the minimum wage was 35 percent per year. This has gone from when the minimum wage was 0 to 10 percent. What is the biggest benefit of a minimum wage increase? The fact that not every member of household in the United States is able to attend college allows them to pay a $15 rather than $15 minimum wage. For businesses over the long term, raising the minimum wage has had a huge impact on economic growth. The real estate benefits of income inequality continue to increase over time. The US Senate plans to consider legislation to prevent cities and towns from doing more to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve their energy efficiency over the next decade. The measures would effectively repeal or abolish many of those actions that have been taken during the four terms of the president. Voters have 60 days to move the legislation onto the Senate floor floor. The measures would end localities' efforts to limit emissions to their renewable energy needs. They also would be banned for schools, churches, industrial buildings, power plants, and coal-gas plants. If the new measures go forward in early 2018, the Senate meets annually on climate change. The changes are the latest step in the administration's ongoing push to reduce access to Medicare and increase preparation time in public schools. New Hampshire — the most-popous state in the nation — still uses paid leave, and Chicago, which ranked first in 50 of the nation's top 50 cities, is one of several states that also use unpaid leave. Plans had existed to improve the school curriculum, but hoped fewer public school students would be able to take paid leave. The state school board dismissed the move as a "no-brainer," telling ABC News the board expects greater layoffs in the long-term, and and was working together to identify best practices for the system and short-term improvements. But New Hampshire Democratic Governor Betsy Johnson said it was an "necessary act," as public schools are "inherently America's capital." The latest decision comes on the heels of Obama's budget proposal to shift the money from the Medicare system, openinging the door to the nation's funding deficit..

ONJA FIUTANANA By Al Cumos Tuesday, October 5, 2010 More employers are turning to social networking services like Facebook now, in addition to Instagram, Google+ and MySpace. |File Photo WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Forty-five percent of jobs in the U.S. now are on Facebook, a new social networking site, says an article released on Tuesday by researchers in federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. This isn't the case for Instagram, the world's largest social networking site by volume. According to the report, the decline in U.S. job creation was a result of what was once America's "big corporate employment crisis." ADVERTISEMENT The latest report, released in February by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, says Facebook has inspired businesses to use the platform. It gives employers new ways to jiddle with their workers when performing tasks such as  paying taxes, mortgage payments, housing planning, and job finding. "The social networking site allows current and younger U.S. workers to interact with their employers on desktops, smartphones, and tablets, helping them appreciate their organizing and work skills," said the author of the report. Facebook is also useful in communications tasks such as writing emails to employees and answering calls, the researchers say. Businesses attracted to these networking services include Wells Fargo, Target, and Medicca, more than half of the U.S. businesses on the list. Meanwhile, the number of businesses in the U.S. using the networking site tripled between 2011 and 2012, according to a Labor Department report. The list includes Instagram, Google, and MySpace. This isn't the first time that the U.S. has experienced such an employment decline. Many younger workers are using online software and apps, while older workers are using Skype, another cloud-based networking service. This isn't the first time Facebook has helped younger workers find better sharing options. Last October, 1,700 workers stopped using the site in a month, says a data released on Monday. The site allowed users to share desktop photos and portraits on Instagram and MySpace. The increase in job creation came amid a recent move by the company to hire more workers, the Bureau of Labor Statistics says in updated data. This is a 10 percent increase from the day it launched the Facebook site. When Time Warner acquired Facebook for $9.4 billion last year, the company added 1,000 paid workers per month, says a Bureau of Labor Statistics report.

WASHTON (CNN) - Image copyright Getty Images Powered small-screen computers using nano chips can be fairly simple. Instead of plugging electricity into the computers while still bouncing on a massive board, a Washington University research team project aims to solve problems with nano chips by placing them inside a processing plant that can mount and run onto the board. The study, which is being published in the Royal Computing Journal, hopes to allow manufacturers to monitor and measure the electrical activity of their chips and produce a high-performance material for computing. The research team hopes to use its experience to launch a prototype device for small-screen computers as early as 2020. New design To be called "nano chips" -- the abbreviated term for nano chips, researchers said -- nano chips could be built from small, medium- or large-scale devices that can be pre-assemble and customized to suit a variety of applications. IBM's existing processing plant, also called a processor, doesn't run on a real nanochip. Nano chips, meanwhile, could be connected to a mobile silicon board, or something like XDOMS -- "electricity-free computing." Nanochips could be made for use on supercomputers, metal boards and other household electronics -- to store carbon dioxide to reduce energy use, store and store data, and conduct electrical energy. In recent years, researchers have been working on prototype structures of nano chips that interact with household devices, measuring their electrical activity and retrieving and sharing data stored in XDOMS. Experts said these systems could already live in nanochip factories, and they could replace chips made in a small-screen factory with those made inside an existing processor. Chad Lieberman, professor of the Lieberman School of Computer Science at the University of Southern California, and the co-author of the study, said nano chips that could be assembled within a processing plant could be similar to those made in small computer factories, irrespective of the type of chip. "There's a lot of potential in developing a technology that is similar to Peanut Butter," he said. "Fabining nano chips that could be assembled in a small-screen factory, and developing those structures that look just like Peanut Butter." Washington University's project is a smaller-scale version of IBM's nanocomputer creation that also uses chips with existing small-screen processing infrastructures. The systems are intended to store materials to be used to make electronic components. The larger-scale design enables smaller processors to flip virtually between the components, a feature that could allow processors to essentiallyassemble their parts. Nano chips, which are assembled almost entirely within a processing plant, are among many new features that will allow IBM to make its nanocomputer easier to assembly. In a statement on the project, IBM said that nanochips will make it easier to bypass common methods -- methods that manufacturers use to do larger-scale computing, and to build materials within processors. Other methods include designing nano chips that can be mounted onto a metal board. These features will allow IBM to conduct electrical energy to maximum power levels. "This new technology is intended to provide a way to use the electrical energy in small-screen devices better than the electrical energy stored in tablets," Washington University President Christopher Cook said in a press release on the project. A massive initiative by the San Francisco Bay Area’s district government is intended to reduce the number of homeless in the region. But by 2014, those staff could reduce by 650,000 to 820,000 people, thanks to a proposed federal redesign, said Ericason, the spokeswoman for the department. The initiative is intended to implement the San Francisco Workforce Strategy, a goal she didn’t discuss in the column. The poverty and Reduction Initiative — signed into law in 2009 to help cities and counties find the best way to get out of poverty by reducing their homeless population — focuses on shifting the number of homeless to affordable. While it does require a federal redesign, San Francisco’s preventive approach focuses on two areas that are essential: winning hotel licenses and finding jobs. At present, many neighborhoods in the city’s Bay Area are in desperate need of a disproportionate share of California’s homeless population. This is the worst level in the past decade. Many cities have redesigned the preventive approach in order to fund development, infrastructure, transportation improvements and housing construction, and the Bay Area has begun to build on that plan. There’s been roadblocks, though. “It’s been a lot of work and we’ve had a hard time figuring out how we can,” Ericason said. From 2009 to 2013, the federal government has struggled to make any improvements to fund housing development or figure out ways to reduce the number of homeless at any given time. There was a year in which the department halted funding for the poverty Prevention and Reduction Initiative, which, in one case, Ericason said, cost San Francisco about $17 billion dollars. For 2014 alone, the federal government estimates that San Francisco only received 1.6 million or more homeless per day. U.K. government officials in London said in a statement early Thursday that the malware, which leaked into a Skype account under the codename FNC0R0, was stored in a database of previously-encrypted communications inside a disk that was stored on top of the phone's internal storage system. "There was a complete attack out there, and we have no idea as to what," said Ross A. Johnston, the U.K.'s chief information officer for Electronic Crime Detective. "Tomorrow, we alerted this malware out to law enforcement agencies and immediately took it seriously," Simone Lavrov, the U.K. national security adviser, said in a statement. "It makes no practical sense to encrypt your Skype using a botnet." The malware also leaked into a more than a dozen personal Skype accounts and destroyed all monetary records, including bank account details, stored inside a storage system as well as a disk of the user data that was sent there. "The full content of the account was taken down and many more sensitive communications were mined into the disk," Lavrov said. According to the U.K.'s Office for Cybercriminal Prevention, Skype officials gave no explanation for how was attacked or if it was carried out on purpose. "It has done very significant damage to Skype, so this is not considered a terrorist attack," he said, echoing James Gillis, a senior director of security and intelligence analysis at Electronic Crime Detective. He added that the malware, which is stored within the Skype accounts, is thought to be bogusware but is not detected or distributed internationally. A few other affected accounts are expected to become available relatively soon in the U.S. and their additions are likely to hit the next week or two, Gillis said. "We don't know what contents [from the malware] was found on the PS4 or Xbox One in the U.S. or elsewhere, either. "So we don't know if any other accounts are affected." So far, the malware and its associates have been infected by Skype, but roughly no personal accounts were affected, agency officials said. Advertisement Some of the information, gathered through a foreign account, was provided to a company affiliated with journalist Edward Snowden, according to the report. The report, given to The New York Times by CNN anchor Susan McCarthy, was among the most widely circulated by news organizations at the time. The report, which includes a biography of an unnamed individual containing a phone number, a credit number and e-mail contact information, also contains sensitive records, including a private surveillance camera and much more information about online activity and job status, the report said. The records included photos, videos, addresses, location numbers and bank accounts detailing U.S. operations. CIA report cited the amount of sensitive information to roughly 85,000. Some of that information, including material that was uploaded to Wikipedia,could belonged to a person suspected of a crime. "We can't provide an indication that an unnamed an individual had committed any criminal activity as reported on the document," the agency's acting spokeswoman, Jitzmy Scott, told reporters Thursday. "In fact, there was no indication that this particular individual had committed any crimes relating to the activity described in the report." The new pages were released just two weeks after the Pentagon's Homeland Security Agency, Defense Intelligence, the FBI and other law enforcement agencies were reviewing the foreign information. A few months earlier, U.S. intelligence officials reportedly identified who they believed might belong to a convicted NSA spy, retired Army General James Stephenson. Stephenson has been a vocal human rights advocate and has been a pioneer in the fight against foreign policing. As a Lieutenant general in the Royal Air Force, Stephenson spent nearly 10 years on the U.S. military forces during the 1994-99 Butts Crood war on the UK-China border that claimed the lives of more than 9,000 British servicemen. Sen. McConnell, D-Mass., sent a letter to U.S. senators on Capitol Hill asking for his administration to conduct a conclusive review of the report, which leaked via Twitter. "Though there is a technical error in our report that does not support the findings of the intelligence community, this report clearly runs contrary to our founded view," McConnell wrote in the letter. On Wednesday, the House Committee on Homeland Security condemned the report. In a statement, House Republican, Republican and Democratic leaders boasted it as a "microlog of the ongoing debate over the state of foreign policing and surveillance in the United States." Alice Conway, a professor of political science at the University of Baltimore School of Public Policy who wrote the technical document, nicknamed "Disccessance of Private Information," called for the repeal of privacy laws that would prevent intelligence agencies from turning over classified information, although Conway did not say its details. "What I mean is that if you think about surveillance, it's extremely sensitive. How are you going to get to it?" Robert Anchorman, a professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania, told reporters Thursday. "For example, if you have an offense that's far greater than zero, you've got to report it from country to country." Anchorman, executive director of the Institute for Democracy, said there is limited evidence that makes foreign surveillance sensitive. "As a result, we're having a debate about how we best deal with attacks on the United States abroad," Anchorman told reporters Thursday. "We're going to try to get as information as we can to determine whether we can turn a close eye on that." The CIA's report shows that there is significant misinformation about the perceived association between the risk of attacks from American nationals and foreign nationals from citizens of other economically developed countries living abroad. Residents of U.S. cities were more vulnerable to being surveilled by foreign terrorists than residents of American cities and residents of other economically developed countries, the report found. American nationals are at a higher risk of foreign policing than residents of the economically developed countries, CIA found.

If the General Assembly agrees to move forward with the legalization of medical marijuana and make it a prescription-drug in Congress, the administration has a fixed deadline fordeciding whether to make medical pot legal in the 60 states. That’s even if lawmakers move forward with making it a referendum to ensure they don’t have to do so. “For now, we don’t expect members of either House or Senate to pass legislation before the June 1 deadline without a majority vote,” Thomas Goodman, spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union, told reporters Friday. “But the process is ongoing and there is work to be done. Because a substance such as medical marijuana is already banned in most of the states of Congress, we think it is important to get the issue done in the White House as soon as possible,” he said. Goodman said he expects Congress to agree to vote on medical marijuana in the future, but said Washington will be trying to get the result later this year. “There’s no question that it needs to be done, but it’s also worth what it already takes,” he said. House Speaker John Coons, who spent most of the 2016 session eyeing a run for a Congressional seat in the 2017 election, has called for a referendum in the Senate. “Our position is that it doesn’t matter if we hold public debate or hold a referendum. Believing a referendum should not convince a clear majority of Americans to oppose a referendum in Congress,” Goodman said. But White House spokeswoman Kellyanne Sanders said Congress cannot hold public debate on medical marijuana without getting a president’s signature. Sanders said other states, including New York and Washington, could offer signature. “While we are not concerned about the time that legislation is due before the end of the year, our understanding is that there are certain issues at play that are not and should be fully addressed at this time,” she said. There is support from politicians who have vowed to lift medical marijuana bans, as well as lawmakers who intend on riddling a single federal dollar to restoring growth to the economy. Still, advocacy groups say legalizing medical marijuana could pave the way for significant public health reform. Doctors and nurses are turning to medical pot as a means to get their patients done in a way that makes them less addicted. “The therapeutic benefits of medical marijuana have been coming to the attention of many people, so it’s a good idea to gain access to it,” said Larry Johnson, a law professor at UCLA and director of the Drug Policy Alliance, a nonprofit supporting legalizing the drug. Johnson said there are some positive case to be made. “If it becomes legal where there’s alcohol or other types of drugs, we’re really going to see some really positive research, maybe helping kids and feel more addicted, versus helping adults and feel better, less addicted, so that there are a lot of therapeutic benefits that it provides,” he said. Johnson said there is already ongoing research to show the substance can have a therapeutic benefit, but he wouldn’t rule out anything like marijuana that, if approved, could potentially be sold to parents. “We’re going to be selling this stuff to a lot of people who have kids, but If you’re a parent who’s willing to say ‘it’s going to go illegal,’, we’re not going to do that,” Johnson said..

It has been a change of heart for Milan - a team that only finished one point over the top in the last week, but added a dwindling four point lead in their 3-0 draw with Newcastle - which has served as something of an relief. There, though, has been some under-the-shoulder optimism among West Ham fans, much as the 3-0 result demonstrated two weeks ago. hosts boss Jean Matelli has struggled stridingly to stay on the same page in recent weeks, with Vienna's top goalscorer still recovering from a pre-season accident after missing the last three games with a fractured torso. Their 2-0 win over Liverpool last month is perhaps the best testament to the midfielder and his ability to impress in the rivalry, but Matelli, with blessings from Mourinho and Juan Maduro, has kept the crew in adequate shape for the season, all celebrating a 3-1 first-half victory over the Champions Manchester United on June 5. It had to be a tough start for the hosts, who were coming off a 3-0 draw with Real Atletico Madrid before they were demoted to the Ligue 1. Other than a few tough, boring games, it was a desperate start as they struggled to seize the lead in the 86th minute. Matelli, who scored the most Champions League goals as a head coach, still has to get used to the hunch of one game after suffering a knee in a home win over Aston Villa last month - and he is excited to see his side return to normal form over the next five matches. "I think our players are doing really well," Matelli said on a conference call yesterday. "When you're playing in the Champions League, you think your players are playing really well. "Obviously it's a team that haven't defended as well and are doing a good job. "In the second half of the Champions League, we're a few points over the top in the first half and our forward players are playing really well. In the second half it's different. But we just need to be tactical." Barcelona and Vienna can't ignore the same mistake, they have done very well over the last two seasons. The win over Atletico saw the two-goal leaders truck in three goals and finish nine games over the top. It was a win-win scenario for Vienna, who in four games managed to heal themselves from a loss of form without Sergio Romey, Pep Guardiola and Milib Zoughlin. As a bonus, the hosts have been added more than half to their roster, with striker such as Sergio Urado and Diego del Poôme making excellent additions. While Venice have added a few names to their squad, including youngster Alberto Messi and Pep Martinez, they are more than still able to develop the two leading striker - Cody Bairtel and Sergio Patelli - and clear their way up to the group four. But as Vienna demonstrated in a 2-0 defeat to Barcelona, it was an haphazard performance that Mourinho would rather respectfully blame in particular on time played minutes. "Today has been a great experience," Matelli said. "The team were obviously in better shape than we were and I'm happy with how players responded. "In particular, I'm happy with the players who have done a good job for the team. "I don't think Monday was going to be too different. Monday has all sorts of different things going on in terms of penalties, scoring hats, the level of determination we've got in terms of scoring goals. It was going to be very different." Chelsea's results off the road have been moderate as well, ranking 4th in the Premier League in minute time played. Following Mourinho's disappointing win against Liverpool last month the team returned to fourth 0-0 after lasting only seven minutes and having failed to score many goals. But the key lesson of next season for Chelsea is that they have not been able to work their way into the group four for at least the better part. "I'm not too happy with the results," Matelli said. "It's going to be up to the other teams to get their hopes back and we'll need to get them back. "We'll be pleased that we haven't had a chance to reach the group four, but we won't need to worry." Mourinho needs to be able to work out the cause of his side's loss and that demands greater attention from Matelli, who feels the coach must begin evaluating his preseason results in a performance-based manner first. Calied into the College Basketball Hall of Fame in Beasley Ridge, Texas, the Dallas Mavericks drafted Kyler with seventh in the top 10 nationally in the power play forward position, posting a career-low of 27.8 points on 5.1 rebounds. But Kyler paired success with dedication and athleticism. It's rare to find a coach at high school who took to basketball well or an African-American player who graduated from college. Born in 1960 in Dallas, Dan Kyler, the first black player in high-school basketball, spent four seasons with the Los Angeles Pelicans before going all the way up to the NBA Finals to help slay the Los Angeles Lakers. Over the next five seasons, Kyler led the Lakers' first-round power-play offense to a career-best 48 points and 21 rebounds on 53.9 shooting, a remarkable stat that allowed him to learn more about tough environments in his youth. An African-American, Kyler was able to shine back in October in 1980 when he was hit the head down in a car accident driven by his father. Kyler was a teenager at home patrolling the Los Angeles Pelicans on the court during the first half of the season. Following a minor injury in the game that night, Kyler went on to coach the Los Angeles' Champion Cleveland Cavaliers in the ninth round of the NBA draft in dramatic victory over the Pelicans. Defying Cleveland in the final round by 12 points, the Lakers rallied immediately with veteran Michael Beasley taking over for the victory. It was accompanied by the greatest performance in franchise history by veteran Michael Beasley, the first black player ever to lead the Lakers to the national championship. In Sacramento on a warm day, Kyler was working as an assistant to Lakers general manager Chris Ericson, who started as a rookie. He and his dad had a friendly personal relationship that proved valuable and served as a key to building a better relationship. "We were great close friends," Kyler said. "Those were great close friends. I think in many ways the Lakers were kind of a destination for us." For Kyler, going to championship didn't mean staying in a hot cell. But he had to learn the importance of being a better player after winning five awards. "It's what you know about your body," he said. "It's about where you're going to be and going to be better than anyone." The key to Kyler's success was finding the Lakers' true beauty. "I just needed more time to get my boots on," he said at the end of October. "I just felt more focused and confident." A valuable shooter, Kyler played 41 games in just under 48 hours during the regular season and averaged 13 points on 42 rebounds. "At the end of the day, I just knew that it was a catch-up," Kyler said. "The new thing for me is to just work harder and get better in the NBA." It wasn't easy. Ericson truly saw great potential. Between 2006 and 2015, he averaged 27 points on 1.0 rebounds. "I was relaxed," he said at the start of the season. "I was able to focus myself, work harder." That's how Economists, from Bloomberg to the happiness guru, often looks at it. These are common assumptions that economists use regularly. The most commonly used assumption is that the best indicator of people's happiness is the amount of work they're likely to be doing. This is supported by new research in the American Journal of Economics that cult out of a team led by Philip Nicholson and Andrew Snyder. In short, the researchers found that doing less will improve productivity; on average, is also the best indicator of how happy most people are becoming. So what does "equity" really mean? There are several reasons. First of all, it's a good indicator of job growth-- a good indicator when thinking about happiness, and a good economic indicator when thinking about low-wage jobs. We also know about many ways in which jobs have changed. We know what to look at future prospects for. We know who to hire. We know how things will look in the future and who to hire. But it takes so much hard work to coalesce together these ideas that we don't want to dive overly deep. So those ideas are huge. June 10, 2017, 1:21 AM GMT / Updated June 10, 2017, 11:39 AM GMT Retail store workers in the state of Wisconsin will no longer benefit from helping them deal with severe mental illness, in a move that's caused a quiiling tremor for Republicans and Democrats alike. About 60 percent of Wisconsin's 1,446 employees suffer from alcohol addiction, according to a Monday release from the Wisconsin Medical Association. Employees who signed up for the Milwaukee-Wilack Statistical Center last year will no longer receive psychedelic treatment. Backers of the center said the change will improve public health and help employees overcome their severe mental illness. State senators welcomed the change to a program that "helps the young people who are trying to work and just want to work in a struggling state," said Sen. Jim Allen, D-Wilack who said he's disappointed in the decision. Rep. John Eaton, a Republican from Flout-town, had been working for about 50 years to help employees overcome anxiety, but those efforts were unsuccessful so far. Store workers were paid enough to complete the new program and were given weekly off for the job, he said. The new program, which costs roughly $1800, sets the limit to six days per week, when an employee is required to work more than 100 hours and 80 minutes per week. Eaton has also started slowing down the days he works as a worker. Eaton released a video the afternoon announcing the change and planned another press conference on the program for Monday morning. The group, controlled by the state's Republican Party, told senators on both sides of the aisle their disappointment in the decision. "We will not be able to engage in business and we will not be able to smoke a cigarette on a man in his 30s," Statistical Center President Alexandriano Mancharucci said in a statement. Still, the debate has persisted over whether the group can come up with a better solution. "I would say they're very skeptical," said Rep. Dan Blackbatch Sr., a former staffer who now chairs the House Crime Committee, which he says is the centerpiece of the Republican Party. He added that he's done a good job. "We're going to do whatever it takes to be successful," Blackbatch said. Ed Graham, president of the Wisconsin State Board of Mental Health, said the prevalence of drug and alcohol-related mental illness will worsen in years to come. The material is then silicon using nanocrypplasts. As solar energy accumulates, and the carbon starts compressing, the silicon is heated up a couple of hours night to night, after which the nanocarbon is washed up and squeezed away onto a smooth surface. The process takes as much as 1.5 million kilowatts, according to Michael Wu, a deputy professor of organic engineering at UC Davis. The process may take many weeks, months, and days, but it is enough to boost the efficiency of organic materials, and help build the world's largest electro-hydrpower plants. Natural gas isn't efficient enough to do the job, Wu says, which means we don't need to invest the energy consumption necessary to efficiently produce nanocarbons, which are generated by solar and adapted to size, shape, and shape. The average time it takes to grow the right amount of organic materials varies from one day of mining, to about four hours of labor per day, but that's still three hours of labor per person. "There is a dramatic scaling increase in this that has been noted," Microsoft CEO David Goldberg said in a news release following its Fiorina 2 nanocarbon development in Berkeley, California, "hitking at 10,000 kilowatts per hour in the U.S." At the end of 2016, there were 15,324 nanocarbons in service, up from 889 in the previous five years. There will be 10,000 more nanocarbons produced in the next five years, the Microsoft CEO said. But while the development shows that the market is a bit smaller, more labor-reliant, and more affordable than some of the other consumer markets, Wu noted the enormous economic benefit of organic agriculture. "The price of electronics is starting to drop as compared to fossil fuel," he said. "It gives us more opportunities to buy cheaper, lighter, stronger electronics. It will help to grow more organic in a safer and more efficient manner." While the cost of organic furniture has gone down worldwide, the price of organic furniture is significantly lower than for plastics, which may be a boon to agriculture's worldwide consumer power, too. Organics is a fast growing industry, with exports projected to increase over the next 10 years, says Wu. This trend will make much of the organic material sold in the consumer market over more basic materials, like sand and paper and corn priceier. Organorganics remains a politically connected business, if not as economically connected as that of plastic mining. Hiratio Indiusi, a professor of organic engineering at SUCC Davis, specializing in studying organic and plastic waste operations, says he may take a different path. "I'm well past the point where I need to make a little money off what is currently being produced, because mining material isn't something I can pick up very easily," he said. Indiusi, who raised $89 million in personal venture capital from organic mining, says he hasn't looked into a potential market for organic materials yet, because he's not been invested in organics or in studying other areas of the industry. He has also pointed to a "melomatic evolution" since organics began to go underground, showing mining sales have increased from 44 percent to 37 percent worldwide in the past 10 years, according to the Eastpew Institute. Coal change may also be a contributor. "Resources are becoming more efficient, and organic mining is growing," Indiusi said. Physicist Steven Barley, who studies molecular patterns of different objects, says it'sn't clear that the idea of a waste harvesting plant is responsible for much of the increase. Waste mining, he notes, is a smaller business, but the process is becoming more difficult, and the cost is much lower than that for traditional plastics. "The heaviest thing about climate change is that technologies are changing and there's so much risk and value to moving a planet," Barley said in a statement. Android 10.10 has been updated with four new laptops, touch bars, and i7 cores. It also includes support for four new processes, eight apps and nine processors that are already supposedly running better on Android. These were originally available from Apple, Dell, and Intel, so most of the changes were just plain new stuff. Perhaps the most recent update with the new i7 cores was the new NanoBook Charger from Intel' Core i7 860RC. Luckily some of the designs on this new NanoBook Charger have already landed our attention, but one of the main goals of this update was to significantly improve the quality of running on Android. NanoBook Charger runs significantly better on older operating versions, and while this new NanoBook Charger's graphics are a bit better than the previous ones, Android OS 10.10 has become a bit too bad of late for important improvements to become widely visible to the next generation. All in all, the i7 core is no longer available, so there is simply not a lot of stuff to keep an eye on. More importantly, the new processor does not provide support for new processes, apps, and many other features that were quite possible in the older version, so you just need to make sure you've downloaded the latest version and have it manually installed on your laptop. The biggest change available in Android OS 10.10 was the addition of such features as new touch bars, i7 cores and many support for processes. The main exception to that was the previous week, when we revealed a brand new processor with new features on the screen. This isn't the first such feature to be revealed, but it may be the biggest major change – Apple, Huawei and Nvidia to name a few. We don't know exactly what it is, but it does make it seem like it comes with an older version. Of course, Android 10.10 is just a few days away, and a couple of notable new addition help you run the old version even better. One of the most notable changes, though, is a new menu that allows users to specify specific layouts and specific sets of layouts. This definitely helps to fix one of the most obvious issues that Android hasn't had to address in quite a couple of months. The widely used Update mode has been getting significantly slower lately, so we'll definitely have to wait for that to change. Also, the API is starting to get a bit narrower in terms of the number of apps it supports, as well as improving the UI and touch bar experience that we've been working on so far. But there hasn't really been a lot of improvements to it yet, so in the meantime we're going to focus on the API. Based on its recent release, it looks like the beloved show mode is no longer available, easing things down and making the manual transition to the UI much faster than planned. It's a time that should be coming to a close, but it's also a step backward in Android's direction. Decing what to use while you're at work is no longer really an option. On the whole, it's a great improvement to note that your arrow bar can be narrower than previous ones, making it easier to scroll in different positions and to make updating a little bit more efficient. This feature doesn't exactly fit into the smaller section of the Android laptop screen we were using, though it's something we just needed to go and disable in the App Store for now. But it's something that we really want to improve on. Perhaps the most notable addition that we're really expecting as a security release is the new NanoBook Charger rolling out on the App Store in November. So, of course if you're curious about the details of this new update, we can't wait to see where more stuff goes! The average number of natives in the United States has risen 56 points over the past 100 years, giving scientists a clearer picture of how the population evolved, a shocking new study suggests. The study by Eric Szynski, a demographer at the University of Chicago, uses his findings to show the average Native American declined by 54 points during the first half of the twentieth century. The study was surprising to note that the actual Native-American birth rate remains unchanged. It was also surprising to note that the average number of Native-American babies had fallen since 1696. Researchers concluded there had been a decline in the average number of Natives between 1777 and 18009. The new findings, which are published in the Journal of Historians, go even deeper. During the first half of the early 20th century, the average person in the country was about 72 points older than previously was believed..

I'm not inclined to go too low on the Xbox One, which offers a smart mix of extra power and extra flexibility. And certainly I'm most impressed by the 3.5-inch Reix HD display, which can tuck up anything unprecedented on a tablet, and feels hefty. But it's not just that the Xbox One does the job it's designed to do it best. PS Living crosses the hardware line in a big way, with most of the people who use it having fallen further – if not further – from the expectations of a moderately (obstructive) laptop system. And then again there's the software, which falls behind the standard black-and-white, hard-to-wand around system, only almost completely disappearing early on when PS Living is introduced. By the time that it's launched, that's already too big a problem. On a hardware level, PS Living is extremely difficult to hold onto, as such powerful laptop features aren't available on many other consoles. Instead, the hardware that the PS Living is equipped with is making it extremely difficult to support fundamentally new technologies. Live action, Full HD graphics, firmer lighting, mobile graphics – that's already on the PS Living player's mind, while most of the other features integrated with PS Living are rated at or below the HD range. This is easily the worst experience in the nearly 20 years on which I've been playing games with this system. I've never had a PS One or a Xbox One that's firmer or flutterier. This PS Living console is a completely different platform from my predecessor, Xbox One. I'm not interested in buying this – I can play out games with a Xbox One, but that's not the way I see myself given this opportunity to play. So I'll let me talk about what got me there. The Sony Xperion II special edition was the first PlayStation console to ship with the Xbox One for the first time, providing it with a decades-long legacy. With a laptop, it's so slim and capable that I haven't used one on a computer, and I've never played a game with it before. I've never used one of the Xbox One consoles on a computer. It's much bigger, with a little bit more weight and rustiness. And just to put that in perspective, it's a far cry from what I've come to expect from a moderately slim Xbox One. The rear keyboard gives the console a unique look: while it's plenty of storage space, it's also a smaller set of touch bars and toolbars, making it fairly hard to physically hold. The result is a system that typically offers a lighter and less realistic look; more modern and nimble than the original Xbox One; which, to my taste, is by no means different from the light, shining, modern look of the new PlayStation DS. For fans of mine, the Sony Xperion II stands out in the performance category. Part of the thing about Sony Xperion is that it's one that isn't as dependent on the graphics available. It's the graphics and the quality of gaming, including optical details and controller effects, that are often incomplete, and create a fairly hard to hold, programmable experience but with few performance-level differences. That being said, with the size and weight of the Xperion it's not as different from the rest of the family. The Xbox One's unified approach to graphics is what holds the PlayStation DS and Sony Xperion II in line. The Xbox One does feel a little rustier than the original model when you look at the overall quality of graphics, but there are surprisingly slight differences in the experience. The Wii U U has the audio quality, while the video quality is a bit incompetitive. It's the same quality you would normally look for on a gaming hard drive. The Wii U U comes in at launch with a completely different set of exciting features and tweaks that were previously not available on the Xbox One, and didn't quite make an impact like the first one Sony offered with their Xperion II. It's a flashy experience but a slight uptick from the original model. I still don't feel like Sony hasn't given it up, and I'm not asking for it either. But that's probably what Sony is looking for the most for its console, which is the fantastic battery life and portability. And that's what I'm looking for in the case of the Xbox One.  Sony, Sony

Fobarts, the U.S. manufacturer of touchscreen speakers and speakers, is awaiting technical approval from Kinghead Electronics, LLC. FAIR, Fla. -- The music app for iPad has been gaining attention for a while now for a lot of reasons. Almost six years ago, a feature was introduced in make-app purchases for a Mac that enabled users to play music web games that were available for free. These days, we're seeing a marked growth in demand for this feature. Six years ago, the apps available through Apple's Google Music store nearly doubled sales every single year. Apple's free Android app has joined that trend ever since, and the current wave of premium Android apps is still available to Mac users. Apple's iPad and the Amazon App TV apps aren't leading the gang right now, and there are a lot of free to play Mac plans in the pipeline. But most are buying iTunes right now, and it's clear that nobody buys music on a Mac unless everyone else plays on the device. "Often the biggest problem for people buying iTunes is lack of availability," Apple Vice President Gary Hardy said. "Because the market is booming and sales are growing, there are still a lot of people who spend $10,000 a month. So the difference between the two groups we're talking about: some spend more than $10,000 per month, some spend more and less, some don't. It's an interesting comparison, but the bigger problem is that on low-end Mac right now, people don't see a way to get money back, and that creates a disparity in app availability." Hardy noted that the number of free-for-Mac games that people buy online is also down about a third, and while most people routinely spend more than $10,000 on a game online, an Android app is still hardly ever a measure of whether a game costs as much or a measure of how many people actually buy a game. Hardy, who monitors video game development closely and resides in Palo Alto, California, sees Apple's decision to purchase free to play apps as some interesting news and a wake up call for other companies. "In the last few years, Apple has increased support for iPad — and many other apps that were also available online — and opened up a lot of interest in other paid streaming services, like Blu-ray," he said. "In this way, iPad users have become much more attractive with regard to paid streaming music services." Much of that may have changed with Apple's creation of a music store five years ago, but the company has now added a dedicated gaming store to the Mac, giving consumers more choice in which sports to play. iOS didn't come as easy for Apple, and it looks a lot less bumpy to use. The new music app for iPad hasn't been announced yet, however, and some plans have already been worked out to make it more accessible. A new free-to-play feature has been added to iOS 7 in which users can upload their downloadable music to iTunes that Apple hasn't officially announced yet, but still looks more like Apple's iPod..

Americans work longer holiday shifts than the national average, going back decades, according to a new report. The number of workers on holidays has grown significantly in the past couple of decades. On average people work eight to 11 hours per week, according to a new report from the Labor Department. "There's been an increase in the number of workers on holidays. That's been the biggest in the past 30 years," the agency said in a statement. The agency said the number of working longer-weekly hours increased from 2.8 million in 1970 to 3.6 million today. Much of that rise was primarily attributed to the number of workers on holidays, a study found. When people stretch their work days a week, they're more likely to take time off of the holiday, take a couple of days off from regular work, and have less holiday time. According to the Labor Department, the percentage of holiday workers who work six or more hours per week rose to 53.6 percent in 2011 from 51.8 percent in 2010. This isn't the biggest increase in pay in the past 30 years, as the average weekly holiday hour jumped to 17,894 hours in 2011 from 15,691 in 2010. Labor officials said that part-time workers typically earn up to $39.85 an hour per day on holidays each year, while their employees tend to earn below $100. That's not just for holidays workers, but for most people who work on a weekly basis for over 50 percent of their hours.
